# Pāthika Sutta (DN 24 (PTS DN iii 1))

**ID:** DN 24 (PTS DN iii 1)  
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Pāthika Sutta  
**PTS:** DN iii 1  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul0.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul0.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Pāthika Sutta* (DN 24, also cited as *Pātika Sutta*), titled *About Pāṭikaputta* in English translation, opens the third division (*Pāthikavagga*) of the *Dīghanikāya*. The discourse is set at Anupiya, where the Buddha sets out early for alms and decides to visit the hermitage of the wanderer Bhaggavagotta [Emmrich 2012]. The narrative centres around Sunakkhatta, a Licchavi disciple who threatened to disrobe and abandon the Saṅgha because the Buddha would not perform miraculous feats for him or explain the primordial origin of the universe [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Rejecting ostentatious displays of asceticism and wonders, the Buddha demonstrates his spiritual pre-eminence.

Cosmological teachings form an important component of the sutta, including a recurring cosmogonic pericope on the dissolution and reintegration of the world [Jennings 1948]. In this account, beings decease from the Radiant realm (Ābhassara) and are reborn in an empty Brahmā mansion (*suñña-brahmavimāna*), dwelling mind-made (*manomaya*), feeding on joy, and luminous—a description repeated nearly verbatim from the *Brahmajāla Sutta* (DN 1) [Jennings 1948; Radich 2007; Yinshun]. In linguistic scholarship, Friedrich Weller analyzed the transliterated names and terms in the Chinese translation of DN 24, arguing from phonological features that its Indic exemplar was preserved in a Prakrit rather than Sanskrit [Levman 2014]. In the Abhidhamma tradition, the text is referenced in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 18.1).

Curated parallels for DN 24 include discourse 15 of the Chinese *Dīrgha-āgama* (DĀ 15) and several Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 32, SF 46, and SF 298).

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: DA 15 阿[少兔]夷; SHT Sutta 32
- Resembling parallels: SF 298; SF 46
- Mentioned in: Kv 18.1 Manussalokakathā

**Sources**

- [Emmrich 2012] Christoph Emmrich, Die kurze, die lange und die richtige Zeit. Temporale Formen von Welt und Erlösung im Suttapitaka (2012) — Quotation and analysis of the opening setting at Anupiya visiting Bhaggavagotta
- [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Account of Sunakkhatta's defection over miracles and cosmogony in DN 24
- [Yinshun] Yinshun, Investigations into Śūnyatā (Ch. 1–2) — Discussion of the empty Brahmā mansion (suñña-brahmavimāna) pericope in DN 24 and its Chinese counterpart
- [Radich 2007] Michael David Radich, The Somatics of Liberation: Ideas about Embodiment in Buddhism from Its Origins to the Fifth Century C.E. (2007) — Analysis of the cosmogonic pericope and manomaya beings recurring in DN 1 and DN 24
- [Jennings 1948] James George Jennings, The Vedantic Buddhism of the Buddha (1948) — Description of the world dissolution and reintegration theory in DN 24
- [Levman 2014] Bryan Geoffrey Levman, Linguistic Ambiguities, the Transmissional Process, and the Earliest Recoverable Language of Buddhism (2014) — Weller's study of Prakrit phonetic features in the Chinese translation of DN 24
